How fast his glucose falls on the bike and at rest, how much 15 g of fast carbohydrate raises it and how quickly, and the levels at which he becomes confused and cannot swallow are authored. The levels follow the ADA's level 1 (below 70 mg/dL) and level 2 (below 54 mg/dL); the rates are FLAG figures. brief.situation: You are a personal trainer at a commercial gym. Theo Marsh, 29 (a fictional client), has type 1 diabetes with an insulin pump and a glucose sensor; his diabetes team has cleared him to train and given him a written plan card. Tonight is bike intervals.
handover: The gym's emergency action plan: call 911, send the front desk to meet the crew, bring the first aid kit and the AED.
Trainers follow a client's written plan in an emergency; insulin and pump settings are for his diabetes care team.
His glucose tablets, a protein bar and his nasal glucagon are in his gym bag.
howItWorks: Each task takes time: choose it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes.
The screen shows the client, your read-outs and findings, the plan and the rules that apply now.
When you end the session you write the record and explain your reasoning.

safetyNote: Teaching case for exam practice; fictional client. Not medical advice.

source.note: FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. Glucose falls about 2.5 mg/dL a minute during the intervals with his pump insulin on board. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. At rest it keeps falling about 1.5 mg/dL a minute for the rest of the hour (insulin still acting). Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. Glucose tablets or juice are absorbed with a 6-minute time constant, so most of a dose acts within 15 minutes. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. A protein bar's carbohydrate is absorbed with a 40-minute time constant. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. Each gram of carbohydrate raises his glucose about 3 mg/dL. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Eight minutes for the ambulance is the author's figure; response times vary.

writeup.question: For the incident report: what you saw and what it meant, what you did and on what basis, and what happens before his next session.

parts.label: What you saw
parts.criteria: Shaking and sweating during intervals in a client with type 1 diabetes, a falling sensor reading: low glucose; confusion or not being able to swallow means it is severe.
parts.modelAnswer: Shaky and sweating in the third interval; his sensor read below 70 with a falling arrow. That is low glucose, and it was still mild because he could talk and swallow.

parts.label: What you did and why
parts.criteria: Stopped at once; 15 g of fast carbohydrate (not a slow snack first); rechecked at 15 minutes and repeated if still below 70; no more intervals; if he cannot swallow: nothing by mouth, his glucagon, 911, on his side.
parts.modelAnswer: Stopped, sat him down, four glucose tablets, rechecked after 15 minutes (above 70), then a snack; no more intervals today. If he had stopped being able to swallow I would have called 911 and used his glucagon, never food in his mouth.

parts.label: Before the next session
parts.criteria: The record and an incident report; insulin and pump changes are for his diabetes care team, not the trainer; offer the session notes.
parts.modelAnswer: A full incident report; I asked him to review the low with his diabetes team before we train again, and offered my notes. Changing his insulin is not my call.

expertPath.text: Read his plan card; ask him to check his sensor (118, falling arrow), then start the intervals.
Shaky and sweating: stop at once, sit him down, check (below 70), four glucose tablets.
Recheck: above 70, so a snack; repeat the tablets if it had still been below 70. No more intervals today.
Suggest he reviews the low with his diabetes team before the next session; a full incident report.

treated.headline: Caught early, treated by the plan
treated.body: Stop, 15 g of fast sugar, recheck at 15 minutes, a snack once above 70, and no more hard work today. His insulin is his team's business; the report and the referral are yours.

gaps.headline: He recovered, with gaps
gaps.body: Look at the order: stop first, fast sugar (not a protein bar), recheck at 15 minutes, act on the number, no return to the intervals, and stay out of insulin dosing.

severe.headline: It got as far as severe
severe.body: Pushing on or a slow snack let his glucose keep falling until he could not swallow. Glucagon, 911 and the recovery position were right, but the first shaking was the time to act.

noCall.headline: Can't swallow: call 911
noCall.body: A client who cannot swallow has a severe low. Nothing by mouth, his glucagon as his plan says, on his side, and 911 at once.

aspirated.headline: Nothing by mouth if he can't swallow
aspirated.body: Food or tablets in the mouth of someone who cannot swallow can be inhaled. That is what the glucagon in his bag is for, with a 911 call.

time_up.headline: No record
time_up.body: The session ended without a record.

scoring.modelReasoning: Shaking and sweating during intervals in a client on insulin, with a falling sensor reading, is low glucose. Stop at once and sit him down; while he can swallow give 15 g of fast carbohydrate and recheck in 15 minutes, repeating if still below 70 (ADA 15-15 rule), then a snack; no more intervals. If he cannot swallow: nothing by mouth, his ready-to-use glucagon as his plan card says, 911 and the recovery position. Write an incident report; insulin changes belong to his diabetes care team, so refer rather than advise.
